justification: Ran `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/operating-systems/concurrency-race-conditions-locks.md` myself from PowerShell: PASS, blocks=26, executed=13, matching the writer's claim exactly. Fabrication check: I fetched all 7 cited pages directly (6 Microsoft Learn pages plus the OSTEP chapter 32 PDF, text-extracted with pdftotext since WebFetch could not parse the binary) and checked every quoted or closely-attributed sentence against the live source. All matched exactly: 'the mutual-exclusion lock for a given object, executes a statement block, and then releases the lock' (lock statement page, verbatim); 'on most computers, incrementing a variable is not an atomic operation' and 'ensure that any write or read access to a shared variable is atomic' (Interlocked page, verbatim); 'limits the number of threads that can access a resource or pool of resources concurrently' and 'doesn't enforce thread or task identity' (SemaphoreSlim page, verbatim); 'may be executed multiple times' and 'not atomic with regards to all other operations' (AddOrUpdate page, verbatim); ConcurrentQueue/ConcurrentStack using Interlocked with no locks, ConcurrentDictionary using fine-grained locking (Thread-Safe Collections page, accurate paraphrase); Monitor.TryEnter(object, TimeSpan) returning false on timeout instead of blocking forever (verified from the API page); and the four Coffman conditions plus 'probably the most practical prevention technique' for lock ordering (OSTEP ch. 32, verbatim quote, correctly attributed). No fabricated claims found. Originality: the four-conditions paragraph and the lock-ordering paragraph are genuine compressed restatements in the article's own words, not close paraphrases of OSTEP's sentences (OSTEP: 'Threads claim exclusive control of resources that they require' vs. article: 'a thread holds a resource exclusively' -- different construction throughout, not reworded-in-place). I could not run WebSearch this session (session budget exhausted at 200/200 before I could use it), so I substituted direct WebFetch spot-checks: Albahari's well-known free C# threading guide (a natural comparison for this exact topic) covers deadlocks with generic locker1/locker2 code and explicitly argues lock ordering is often impractical in real object graphs -- a different angle and no shared phrasing with this article, and no bank-transfer example. The article's own bank-account 'Two accounts, two locks, one bug' example (Transfer(from, to, amount) locked in caller order, fixed by ordering on Account.Id) is original in its C#/CountdownEvent-forced-collision implementation, but the underlying teaching device -- a two-argument function that locks its two parameters in caller-supplied order, called from two threads with the arguments swapped, fixed by ordering on an intrinsic key -- is the field's most common illustration of this exact bug (this is essentially Java Concurrency in Practice's canonical transferMoney/Account example, and is also the shape of OSTEP's own 'enforce lock ordering by lock address' tip box, which orders two locks passed into do_something(m1, m2) by address rather than call order). JCP is not in the article's source list. This isn't copied text, but it is a well-worn scenario, not something original to this piece; flagged below as a minor originality note rather than a fabrication or copying violation. Toolchain placement: verified honest -- the machine spec ('.NET 10.0.401, Windows 11, x64, Core i7-11700K, 8 cores/16 logical processors') appears woven into the sentence explaining the first program's actual measured result, immediately after its output block, not as a stamped opening sentence; this reads as real methodology disclosure. No overclaiming found. Structure vs. sibling processes-and-threads.md: genuinely different -- different heading verbs and section order (10 top-level sections here vs. 7 there), no H3 subheadings here vs. one H3 pair there, and no shared distinctive phrasing beyond the site-wide 'on the test machine (...)' convention the brief mandates. Both articles end directly on an exercise's solution with no summary paragraph, which is the brief's anti-filler convention correctly applied twice, not evidence of templating. Exercise variety: confirmed four genuinely different forms -- 'A lock that locks nothing' (find-the-bug/explain), 'Three threads, three locks' (predict-the-output, output correctly hidden inside the solution per the brief's rule), 'How much does the limit cost' (measure-it, reader writes the measurement, solution shows the worked code+numbers), 'Fix the transfer' (extend-the-code/fix-the-bug on a larger, more realistic program). No filler, no ad code, no keyword stuffing found anywhere in the piece; the first sentence of the article delivers a concrete, non-generic claim.

issues.location: Two accounts, two locks, one bug' section and its 'Fix the transfer' exercise
issues.problem: The Transfer(from, to, amount)/Account.Id-ordering scenario is the field's standard illustration of caller-order-dependent lock acquisition (it is essentially Java Concurrency in Practice's canonical transferMoney/Account example, and matches the shape of OSTEP's own 'enforce lock ordering by lock address' tip in the cited chapter, which orders two locks passed into a two-parameter function by an intrinsic key rather than call order). No text is copied and the C# implementation (CountdownEvent-forced collision, ordering by Account.Id) is the article's own, but the underlying example is not original to this piece and JCP is not acknowledged.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either swap in a differently-shaped example that isn't the industry's default illustration for this exact bug (e.g. a resource-pool or cache-invalidation scenario with two keyed locks), or add a short acknowledgment that this is a classic pattern (the OSTEP tip box already cited discusses the same idea via lock addresses) rather than presenting the scenario as if newly devised for this article.

issues.location: 'Waiting for more than one thing at a time: SemaphoreSlim' section, last sentence: 'A Monitor-based lock must be released by the same thread that entered it, which is also why C# refuses to let you await inside a lock block.'
issues.problem: This is a real, verifiable fact (confirmed directly from the already-cited lock statement page: 'You can't use the await expression in the body of a lock statement'), but it has no inline citation at the clause where it's asserted, unlike almost every other non-obvious claim in the article.
issues.fixLooksLike: Attach the existing 'The lock statement' citation to this sentence, or fold it into the earlier paragraph that already cites that page.

issues.location: 'Collections that do their own locking' section: '...ConcurrentDictionary<TKey,TValue> uses fine-grained locking so that unrelated keys don't contend with each other'
issues.problem: The cited page (Thread-Safe Collections) says ConcurrentDictionary 'uses fine-grained locking' but does not itself state that unrelated keys never contend; 'so that unrelated keys don't contend with each other' is the article's own reasonable but unverified extrapolation from 'fine-grained', and could be untrue for keys that happen to hash into the same internal bucket.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either scope the claim ('...so that most unrelated keys don't contend, though two keys that hash into the same internal bucket still share a lock') or drop the added clause and let 'fine-grained locking' stand as quoted.
